compression.title: Fairwork Cloudwork Ratings
compression.lede: are the Fairwork project's league table of cloudwork platforms, each scored out of 10 on ten thresholds against five principles of fair work (2025 report; Labor Vector record); a missing point means no evidence was found, not non-compliance (2025 report).

sentences.text: The Fairwork Cloudwork Ratings are a rating programme, a league table scoring cloudwork platforms against the five Fairwork Cloudwork Principles, each platform scored out of 10 on ten thresholds, two per principle (Labor Vector record); the 2025 ratings, in their authors' words, assess and score "basic standards of fairness in working arrangements on 16 cloudwork digital labour platforms" on fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation (the 2025 report).

The Labor Vector census asks of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" and places this one on four of its five intersections, labor producing AI, gains and losses, worker power and AI governing labor, with two kinds of evidence, rating against standards and worker testimony (Labor Vector record).

The project behind the ratings "studies working conditions on digital labour platforms and rates individual platforms based on their fairness to workers", its goal to show that "better and fairer platform jobs are possible" (the 2025 report); the trade press gives the 2025 edition as an assessment of 16 widely used platforms on five core principles (The Global Recruiter), and a Fairwork video asks "How fair are freelance and remote work platforms?" (YouTube, title only).

Cloudwork, in the report's definition, is work "that can be performed remotely through a digital labour platform", set against location-specific "geographically tethered work" (the 2025 report); it runs from microwork such as data labelling and processing, AI training and image categorisation to freelance services such as translation, web development or design (the 2025 report; the home page), and the census takes it as the labour object, naming the AI data work the report finds done for leading AI companies (Labor Vector record).

Cloudworkers are "generally classified as self-employed or independent workers on paid piece rates" (the 2025 report), whom the census records as supplying the labour, while the platforms rated and the requesters or clients who post work on them direct it (Labor Vector record).

A growing sector of cloudwork is "data services for artificial intelligence development in international supply chains", its clients among the world's leading AI companies, "such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia" (the 2025 report); the trade press calls many cloudwork tasks "fundamental for developing AI systems" (The Global Recruiter), and Fairwork AI states: "There is nothing “artificial” about the immense amount of human labour that builds, supports, and maintains AI systems" (Fairwork AI).

Of the workers of this class the archive holds that content moderators "perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible", meaning being produced "by bodies, at metabolic cost" (#18), and that the labour of content moderators and of "the data labelers performing RLHF" is extracted, its non-compensation borne materially (#623).

The archive calls this ghost work "ground-truth labor", "the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", distinct from variance-generative labor, and holds that ghost work scales and "is paid badly" (#163).

It counts annotators among the sources of semantic labor whose concealment is "the first marker of extraction" (#533), finds the literature of hidden AI labour stopping "at task-labor — annotation, moderation, the edge-case fix", naming the erased worker but not "that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144), and derives the semantic proletariat through moderators and annotators while holding that it is not "AI annotators" or "gig workers" (#1545).

The ratings rest on desk research, worker interviews and surveys, and interviews with platform management (the 2025 report); where managers do not engage, scoring is limited to desk research and worker surveys, and final scores are decided collectively by the core team and peer-reviewed (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), platforms being given a chance to respond and earning points "only if they meet the criteria for each principle" (the home page), with the report, a platform search tool and the Principles and methodology pages as the data (Labor Vector record).

The survey of what the report calls "this third report" was collected between February 2024 and January 2025 and left responses from 776 workers in 100 countries (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

The governing limit is the authors': "Failing to achieve a point does not necessarily mean that a platform does not comply with the principle in question; it simply means that the research team did not find any evidence and/or they were unable to prove its compliance" (the 2025 report), which the census carries as a stated limit and as the negative tag "NOT a finding of non-compliance where a point is missing" (Labor Vector record); and the surveys "do not aim to build a representative set of experiences" but seek to understand how work is carried out and managed (the 2025 report), "NOT a representative survey of cloudworkers" in the census's tag (Labor Vector record).

In 2025 ComeUp, Elharefa and Translated scored 8, Creative Words and Terawork 7, Prolific 5, SoyFreelancer 4 and Appen 3, and the remaining eight no more than 2, three of them with no point evidenced (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), Upwork at 1 and Amazon Mechanical Turk, Freelancer and Microworkers at 0 (the 2025 report's league table), and the census sets Turkopticon beside the record as its neighbour (Labor Vector record).

No platform reached 10, which only Creative Words has ever done, once, in 2023 (the 2025 report); the executive summary counts "the remaining nine platforms" where the key findings and the table give eight, an inconsistency the census records (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), and the operator's cloudwork page lists the 2025 scores without Creative Words, Terawork its one platform at 7 (Fairwork cloudwork page).

Seven platforms evidenced systems to pay workers on time for all completed work, and four, ComeUp, Translated, Elharefa and Terawork, met the threshold "that the majority of workers should earn at least the local minimum wage" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), four of 16 "after costs" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter).

Nine platforms met the threshold on measures against unreasonable competition, overwork and unpaid labour, and for most no evidence was found that their terms are free of waivers of the right to legal recourse (the 2025 report); over half, the trade press reports, carry clauses such as "vague job descriptions, blanket liability clauses" (The Global Recruiter).

Six platforms received the point for recognising and engaging collective workers' bodies and none the second, collective governance or bargaining (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); six "now formally recognise the right to organise – up from just 2 last year", none actively bargaining, and seven of 16 guard against risks "such as burnout or back pain" (The Global Recruiter), where the principle asks platforms to "be prepared to cooperate and negotiate" with workers' collective bodies (the home page).

The census finds no intersection with Labor Vector's instruments stated by the resource and reads the ratings as scoring "the intermediary that directs cloudwork (allocation, rejection, deactivation, contract terms)", thresholds 1.1 and 2.1 standing as "the report's own measures of unpaid labor" in its terms (Labor Vector record).

The authors attribute the growth in platforms acknowledging freedom of association to "Fairwork’s engagement" and count a record 56 changes by eight platforms, estimated to affect over two million workers (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), made "Through direct engagement" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter), as the 2023 text on the operator's page found platforms incorporating fairness "as a result of engagement with Fairwork researchers" (Fairwork cloudwork page).

Of the surveyed workers 31.2% reported non-payment and 38% late payment, Global South workers report "discrimination and distrust when competing with workers from other regions" (the 2025 report), a line the Capture Registry finds in the report (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and of 448 respondents 33.3% put the local minimum wage first and 18.3% payment for all completed work (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

The report finds platforms' own governance initiatives "insufficient in most cases to ensure basic compensation rights", cites platform work studies on how "algorithmic management accentuates opacity in decisions affecting workers" (the 2025 report), and its co-lead holds that voluntary improvements "will never be enough" (Valente, in The Global Recruiter).

On the census's reading the ratings answer whether a named platform shows evidence of meeting each threshold, which policies changed in the scoring dialogue and which rights surveyed workers rank highest, and do not answer the market-wide share below minimum wage, whether a platform with no point violates the principle, or the conditions of AI data work at outsourcing companies outside the platforms rated (Labor Vector record).

Who gains is "not recorded as a quantity" (Labor Vector record); in the census's worked questions the entity holds pay and conditions against minimum standards and platforms rated with a survey of 776 cloudworkers, while no record measures how gains divide among workers, employers, platforms and model providers, or how much of a system's training data any reported work produced (Labor Vector record).

The project is based at the Oxford Internet Institute and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center and financed by, among others, the BMZ, commissioned by GIZ, its five principles developed in 2018 at a multi-stakeholder workshop at the ILO and its cloudwork principles in 2020 (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); the WZB calls Fairwork its joint project with the Oxford Internet Institute (WZB), and the certification site calls it "A non-profit spun out of the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) & Berlin Social Science Center (WZB)" (fair.work).

Of the earlier editions, the WZB reported the 2022 ratings, 15 platforms with the top score seven of ten (WZB), King's College London's portal holds that report, 34 pages, as "Work in the Plenatary Labour Market" (King's College London; its abstract), the operator's page carries 2025, 2023, 2022 and 2021 and still shows the 2023 text of 15 platforms (Fairwork cloudwork page), and Fairwork recorded the 2023 launch (YouTube, title only); the census gives the 2025 report as the third cloudwork report, with earlier reports in 2021 and 2023 (Labor Vector record), and the report calls itself both "this third report" and "this second cloudwork league table" (the 2025 report).

Beside the ratings Fairwork runs strands the census keeps apart: national location-based rankings in 38 countries and principles for the fair use of AI in the workplace (the home page; Labor Vector record), and a certification of the firms that commission AI data work, "based on evidence including the voices of the workers themselves" (fair.work), announced in the report to AI lead firms (the 2025 report), whose Fair Pay principle asks for "the local living wage after work-related costs" (fair.work).

The authors declare no connection with any platform and no conflict of interest and note sections in common with other Fairwork reports, and Scale/Remotasks, in its comment, holds the evaluation "overly subjective in key areas" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

At the name the Capture Registry finds the programme held, its principles, scale, 16 platforms and operator the record's, reads "spun out of" as the composition's word for an operator the record gives as based at both, and gives the innocent reading first: the Overview gives the ratings' publisher, principles, scale and general findings and offers a platform's score (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It finds the scores absent, "A rating programme is composed by its principles and its general verdict, without its ratings", the composition keeping "the standard" and dropping "the platforms it was applied to", the improvement given "without its cause", neither caveat reaching it, what the ratings are for left out, and one card, fair.work, drawn from another strand (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The record landed on laborvector.org the same day and no card cites it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the census leaves unchecked the Principles and methodology pages, the search tool, the AI Principles and the earlier reports (Labor Vector record), and Wikipedia has no article on the ratings or on Fairwork (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

O18-01.quote: Content moderators perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible. … Meaning is not "immaterial." It is produced by bodies, at metabolic cost, under conditions of potential harm.
O18-01.source_label: #18 The Semantic Economy: A Marxian Accounting Framework for the Production, Extraction, and Exhaustion of Meaning as Value
O18-01.locus: Part I §I.4d, ¶ after the review of Gillespie, Roberts and Qiu (para 28)

O623-01.quote: Second, semantic extraction has real consequences for real workers. The Wikidata volunteers, the content moderators, the data labelers performing RLHF — their labor is extracted, and they experience the effects of non-compensation materially.
O623-01.source_label: #623 Semantic Infrastructure: From Tim Berners-Lee to the Semantic Economy — Bridging Technical and Political-Economic Frameworks
O623-01.locus: the second reason, on semantic extraction and workers (para 71)

O163-01.quote: Ghost work is *ground-truth labor*: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true. The labor type at issue here is *variance-generative labor*: the labor of producing new conceptual structures that the model cannot generate from its own distribution.
O163-01.source_label: #163 The Neglected Author as Tail-Preserving Labor: A Coupling Hypothesis on Recognition Bias, Tail-Renewal Value, and the AI-Era Decoupling of Uptake from Consecration
O163-01.locus: § on the labor architecture of AI (para 40)

O163-02.quote: Ghost work scales: more workers labeling more images produces more training data of the same kind. … Ghost work is paid badly; variance-generative labor is not paid at all because acknowledging it as labor would require acknowledging the producer as a sovereign source.
O163-02.source_label: #163 The Neglected Author as Tail-Preserving Labor: A Coupling Hypothesis on Recognition Bias, Tail-Renewal Value, and the AI-Era Decoupling of Uptake from Consecration
O163-02.locus: § on the labor architecture of AI (para 40)

O533-01.quote: Map each source of semantic labor — participants, annotators, integration engineers, compliance teams, users who re-prompt and re-frame. If the framework does not name these sources, the bearing-cost is concealed. Concealed bearing-cost is the first marker of extraction.
O533-01.source_label: #533 The Groundskeeper's Treatise: A Diagnostic Reading of Platform Stewardship Theory through the Semantic Economy

O144-01.quote: *Where it stops:* at task-labor — annotation, moderation, the edge-case fix. … It names the erased worker; it cannot name that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE PROGRAMME HELD. The five principles, the scale out of ten, the 16 platforms of the 2025 report and the operator (based at the OII and the WZB) are the record's;

CAP-1-08.quote: The innocent reading first. The Overview gives the ratings' publisher, principles, scale and general findings from the project's own reports, and offers a platform's score.

CAP-1-04.quote: THE SCORES ABSENT. The ratings exist to score named platforms: … The composition offers 'a specific platform's score' and gives none.

CAP-1-09.quote: A rating programme is composed by its principles and its general verdict, without its ratings.

CAP-1-10.quote: The record's unit is the platform score, and the scores are what name who directs the labour and on what terms; the composition keeps the standard and drops the platforms it was applied to.

CAP-1-05.quote: The composition gives the improvement without its cause.

CAP-1-06.quote: THE CAVEAT ABSENT. The record's negative tags keep a missing point apart from a finding of non-compliance ('failing to achieve a point does not necessarily mean a platform fails the principle') and keep the surveys apart from a representative sample. Neither reaches the composition.

CAP-1-12.quote: Purpose absent: the composition gives what the ratings do and find, not what they are for (to show better and fairer platform work is possible).

CAP-1-07.quote: A CARD FOR ANOTHER STRAND. The fair.work card is Fairwork's certification of 'the labour behind AI', a separate scheme the record names (its AI supply chain certification).

CAP-1-11.quote: A baseline: the record landed on laborvector.org the same day (commit bf90841) and no card cites it. NEW address.
